June 28, 1977,-That Bill C-51, an act to amend the Criminal Code, the Customs Tariff, the Parole Act, the Penitentiary Act and the Prisons and Reformatories Act, be amended in clause 3 by striking out lines 47 to 49 at page 3 and lines 1 to 8 at page 4 and substituting the following therefor:

He said: Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few comments in connection with this amendment. Effectively, what it provides for is to remove subsection (b)(i) and renumber (b)(n) as (b). Subsection (b)(i) reads as follows:
(b) any firearm that

The reason for this amendment was set forth very well in the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, which can be found in issue No. 18 dated June 2, 1977. I should like to refer to what Mr. L. H. Nicholson, the chairman of the firearms legislation committee, said at page 18:8, which reads as follows:
The next item is the definition of "restricted weapon". This is a new definition of a restricted weapon. It would include one that is semi-automatic or self-loading, discharges centre-five ammunition and has a barrel under 18.5 inches in length. It is understood that the purpose here is to provide some control over the M-l carbine, an arm now favoured by criminals, but unfortunately it also covers other makes and other models in significant numbers now used by good citizens in hunting. The change proposed will prevent the further use of these firearms and it will cause a substantial loss to the present owners because they can no longer use them for hunting. The provision is therefore strongly opposed. As to the makes and models to which I refer and their numbers, I have some further information if it is of interest to the committee.
At page 18:16 the committee report indicates Mr. Nicholson referring to various rifles. He continued by saying, "I could go on; I have another half dozen."
There are numerous guns with barrel lengths that are under the 18'/2-inches referred to in this subsection. If this subsection is passed, it will mean that many people throughout Canada will have rifles which will immediately become restricted weapons. These people have had these guns in their possession for many years and have used them when partaking in sports and hunting. To bring in this particular clause would have the effect of putting all these people in a position where they are breaking the law, which is not the intention of the legislation. 1 am advised by the Saskatchewan Wildlife Federation that in many instances people have rifles with barrel lengths slightly over 18'/2 inches. If they damage the muzzles of those guns, they have to be taken to a gunsmith to be worked on, and they end up with barrels of less than 18'A inches and therefore would fall within this particular section.
The attempts to restrict the use of the M1 carbine can certainly be carried out by subsection (d) on page 4 of Bill C-51, which reads as follows:
-a weapon of any kind, not being a prohibited weapon or a shotgun or rifle of a kind that, in the opinion of the governor in council, is reasonable for use in Canada for hunting or sporting purposes, that is declared by order of the governor in council to be a restricted weapon.
It seems to me that under subsection (d) the governor in council could make the necessary order restricting the weapons it desires to restrict, thus leaving the hunter and the sportsman free to own, possess and use the guns to which I have referred. I am not happy with any legislation, particularly in the Criminal Code, which gives the governor in council the right to pass legislation which is never debated in this House. Mr. Speaker, 1 support the amendment of my colleague, the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil). I know a considerable number of people who own carbines. In fact, I have one myself which I received many years ago. I have not measured the barrel, but I suspect it is somewhat less and would probably fall into this category. It is hard to imagine it being more dangerous than any other weapon. In fact, if a weapon is longer than ISV2 inches, it could be sawed-off by anyone who wished to use it as a criminal weapon.
As I understand the legislation, the government wants control over the M1 carbine. However, I believe that any weapon should be put into the pre-emptive weapon code by order in council. It should be placed there as a restricted weapon, rather than a blanket provision cutting out all guns that fall under this classification. To outlaw all of these guns is not the best way to approach this problem, particularly when vast numbers are already in the hands of people. This is a popular sporting weapon. Presumably, if you have a gun 19 inches in length, it would fall within the legal category. The carbine is an easy gun for a sportsman to carry. I have found it extremely easy to carry. It is a very popular gun. It is light, and it is good in dense bush.
If a particular weapon is being used extensively by criminals, the best way to deal with that problem would be through subclause (d). I strongly suspect there would then be more co-operation from the sporting groups. This could be publicized through wildlife groups which encompass almost everyone in the sporting field. It would be given wide publicity that it is a prohibited weapon. By taking the public more into its confidence, there would be a better law.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1977 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, want to go on record as supporting the amendment of the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil). I have received many representations from constituents regarding the length of the gun barrel. I strongly support the hon. member's argument that in many instances, due to lack of accuracy of guns, one-quarter to one half-inch is taken off at the muzzle. This usually causes some damage at the muzzle. The best way for a gunsmith to repair the damage and the accuracy is to shorten the barrel, probably by less than one inch. That makes it an illegal weapon under this act. In most cases, these guns have been in the hands of the family for years. Immediately placing them on the restricted list will prove a hardship.

This points out the whole scope of this type of regulation or law which the government of Canada tries to bring in that deal with gun control. It is very easy to bring forward such laws, but very difficult to make them do what they are supposed to do. Any law to control guns in Canada must be aimed at the criminal element. This is where the problem usually begins. The Liberal government is trying to bring in some kind of gun control that will control guns in the hands of people whom they believe should not have them. I do not know how they will be able to do that in a responsible manner. Those they are aiming at, people who use guns as weapons for their defence, in anger or other uses, will get these guns, at any rate, in one way or another. I agree with the hon. member for Moose Jaw that trying to control the Ml carbine should be done under subclause (d). It should not be done by taking away from responsible people in Canada something that they have not used in a criminal or irresponsible manner but have kept in good working condition.
When you look at the bill, you see that all the gun control is being done by regulation. It is all done by order in council. That is one reason so many people in Canada are up-tight about this bill. Nothing is really spelled out other than a few areas such as regulating the length of the barrel. I do not think we want to pass laws in this House that will make criminals out of people. It is very honourable to pass laws which attempt to control the criminal element-an element in Canada that needs a lot of control. It is unfortunate that we have them and that they have to be controlled. I do not really believe that we should be making laws that make criminals out of innocent people. I am referring to people who have cut down the length of the barrel of their guns to improve the accuracy of their shooting or to repair a damaged muzzle.
I know that it does not destroy a gun to shorten the length of the barrel but, rather, makes for more accurate shooting. We are talking here about changing a section so as to allow people to make changes to their Ml carbines, and I hope we will not pass this section as it stands, which would make criminals out of innocent people. Some people might not even know that such a law has been passed by the House of Commons in Ottawa and that their rifles are illegal under the new regulations. The barrel of the rifle could have been shortened years ago by someone in the family, and the gun handed down in the family. Suddenly, a regulation is passed in Ottawa and the fact that the gun had been shortened by a quarter of an inch, half an inch, or even one inch, makes the owner a criminal. We know what happens to people who are in trouble with the law.
The people we want to control are those who are deliberately out to break the law, who do not respect the law. There can be a larger number of rifles in the possession of innocent people who will find themselves in contravention of the law as a result of this section of the act. That is the reason I strongly support the amendment of the hon. member for Moose Jaw.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 should like to say a few words on this amendment to a clause which has been considered very thoroughly and carefully ever since the introduction of Bill C-83, over a year ago. The question is the limiting in the statute of high-powered, rapid-fire weapons with a barrel length of less than 18'/2 inches. I think that when we are looking at matters of gun control we have to weigh and to balance the public interest against private interests. As I have said, we considered this matter very carefully with firearm experts in the RCMP and others.
Recently, even subsequent to the bill being reported from committee, I met with Colonel Nicholson of the Canadian Wildlife Federation. He came to me on this issue and pressed his case and the case of those who wanted this amendment. As a result of Colonel Nicholson's further visit, I re-examined the whole situation as late as last Thursday and Friday, and in my view the legislation as proposed should stand.
The purpose of this provision is to restrict rapid-fire, con-cealable weapons. Obviously, a weapon with a short barrel length is easily concealable under a raincoat or a trench coat if the stock has been sawed off. Police records indicate that a large number of short-barrelled guns are being used for criminal purposes. The Ml was developed during the Second World War as a personnel stopper. The AR-15 was designed and produced for use in the Vietnam war and these guns are now being used widely by criminal elements in the United States and in this country. Therefore, as a matter of public policy it seems to me that we should endeavour to restrict their availability and use in Canada as much as possible.
It would be contrary to the rules, but I wish 1 could bring into the House the kinds of guns we are talking about. I did show those guns to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, and 1 think the committee was impressed by what we were talking about.
I met very recently with the Kelowna District Fish and Game Club. 1 showed its members the kinds of guns we are talking about. Once they knew the kinds of guns involved, they supported this bill and this proposal to restrict semi-automatic, centre-fire rifles of barrel lengths of less than 18I/2 inches. I have examined gun catalogues. 1 examined the list Colonel Nicholson produced to the committee. The list submitted included short-barrelled .22s which are not restricted under this provision. It included a number of weapons that by no conceivable definition could be considered hunting weapons. The Plainfield Machine Company carbine has a collapsible stock. It was designed as a military weapon and it is ideal for criminal purposes, but quite unsuitable for sporting purposes. If hon. members were able to see pictures of such weapons, let alone the guns themselves, I think they would readily agree that these really have no proper public use in this country.
With regard to the aspect of hunting, I point out to hon. members that last month in Saskatoon there was a meeting of the association of provincial hunter-safety training co-ordinators. This association is composed of provincial officers who

June 30, 1977
Criminal Code
operate within the ministries of natural resources and tourism or their counterparts in each of the provinces, and those officers are responsible for the development of gun safety programs and their operations in the provinces.
It was the unanimous view of the provincial administrators of gun safety programs that this type of provision should be in the law and that it should be supported. I refer to the restriction of less than 18'A-inch, rapid-fire or semi-automatic centre-fire weapons. I suggest that there is no proper hunting use for these guns. That was the view of the provincial administrators. Many of these guns are of low calibre and would wound more deer than they would ever kill. Some of them are quite inaccurate in terms of target. They are not good shooting weapons. I could bring before the House a stack of textbooks on rifles and guns indicating that these particular weapons serve no useful hunting purpose.
I want to make it clear that for sporting purposes the present owners of these guns will be able to register them and use them for sporting purposes, that is, for target purposes as part of the regular activities of game clubs. However, when we consider the fact that these weapons are not suitable hunting weapons, and when we consider that they are widely used for criminal purposes and are ideal for criminal purposes, I think we should resist this amendment and implement this provision in the bill.
Hon. members have suggested that we should do this by regulation, but I resist that. Some have criticized this bill by saying it has too many regulations, but in the committee I think we were able to show that the regulatory power under this bill is much more restricted than it was in Bill C-83. The problem with accepting the suggestion of the hon. member from the Okanagan would be that the governor in council would be restricting specific types and names of rifles, and in a very short time neither gun dealers, gun owners, nor the police would know which guns are restricted and which are not.
The demand over the last year has been that there be as great a degree of certainty as possible so that gun owners, gun dealers and the police will know what is legal and what is not, what is restricted and what is not, and what is prohibited and what is not. If we were to accept the suggestions of the hon. member and deal with short-barrelled guns by way of regulation, I submit that in a very short time there would be very great confusion as to which guns were restricted and which guns were not. I do not think gun owners or the police want that result, and I submit that on reflection hon. members would not want it either.

Mr. Speaker, 1 want to put something on the record that has always impressed me. 1 have not been a great student of political science, but I should like to refer to a quotation of the late William Lyon Mackenzie King when he sat in opposition to the Conservative government led by the late R. B. Bennett. On one occasion he said:
Now let us come to another point which I wish particularly to stress. I refer to the right set out in Magna Carta that no man shall be disposed of his rights without the lawful judgment of his peers under the law of the land; not the law as made by the governor in council, not the law as made by some unnamed and as yet unexisting body, but the law of the land as known to everyone. It is an essential principle of liberty and freedom that the law of the land should be known, that it should be so known that every man as he runs may read. speechtext: That is correct. As Mackenzie King said, it is an essential principle of liberty and freedom that the law of the land should be known. We are entitled to know the law. The minister said the police must know what weapons are prohibited. I would be far happier if ordinary people knew what weapons are prohibited or restricted. subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1977 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext: More than likely it was a put-on.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1977 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
I hope it was more than that. If ever an amendment to a bill deserves the support of parliament, it is this one-because the government has a majority: it thinks it can do as it wants. Mr. Speaker, all governments come and go, but the principle of the rule of law remains. I say, inasmuch as 3,300 orders in council were passed, but only 600 published, Canada is in a sorry state. My remarks apply not only to this bill; they apply also to the human rights bill, the immigration bill, and others. This House grinds out bills like a legislative mill. In this case, parliament is erecting the frame of the House, but the executive will put on the siding and roof.
Parliament will legislate power for the executive to make laws while Canadians sleep. Mr. Speaker, we are dealing with a serious subject, the criminal law affecting the rights and liberties of the individual. I never thought I would see the day when a provincial legislator would be jailed for his refusal to divulge information. That was shocking. You cannot do your job without information. Sometimes you must get it surreptitiously because you cannot pry it out of this government. What happened to that legislation could happen to any Canadian on the strength of an order in council passed in secret.
I expect the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) remembers the time when this House debated a spy inquiry which involved certain civil servants. It was alleged that there was no law to cover the matter, and the minister of justice of the day passed an order in council whereby people were incarcerated. Lights in their cells were left burning. That minister said it was an emergency and passed the order in council. Surely there is no emergency so great that we can put in jeopardy the rights and freedom of the individual, as certain dictators in Europe did. You cannot put them in jeopardy by passing an order in council. Therein lies the great danger of this bill.
I want parliament to debate such orders in council; to examine them. That is why I propose my amendments. The

first of them concerns the appointment of peace officers by order in council. Perhaps the point is not too serious, although the Casal group appearing before the committee wanted that provision changed. I ask hon. members to support motion No. 28 which will provide for orders in council relating to the criminal law to be brought before parliament.
Before I sit down, let me make one more point. Many people wrote to the chairman of our committee and to me asking for the opportunity to testify on this bill. I do not know why there was such a great rush in pushing this bill through committee. Sometimes we sat from early morning to late at night, but most people were denied the opportunity to testify. The Committee heard several small groups. The Advocate Society of Upper Canada, including benchers of Ontario, appeared before the committee. We listened to Messrs. Chappell, Cartwright and Cooper, distinguished scholars all from Toronto. They warned the government of the consequences of amending the criminal law as the bill proposes. I shall have more to say later about the invasion of privacy provisions, which are a disgrace. I am asking parliament, in a non-partisan way, to examine seriously how the government intends to enact criminal law by order in council passed by some unnamed body or unnamed person perhaps some time in future. It may be my lot to be that person, but I do not want that responsibility. 1 want Canadians to know where they stand. I want our law-abiding citizens to be protected by the law and to know the law. Because if they do not know the law, how do they know they are breaking it?
I will say no more lest I should undo my own case-which has happened in the past. I think my case is strong; I have tried to make it sincerely and intelligently. As a practising member of the Saskatchewan and the Alberta bars of 30 years standing, and as a trial lawyer, I know how these things work. I have defended people charged with contravening the wartime prices and trade regulations at a time when orders in council were ground out by the thousand and nobody could be certain of the law. People were brought before the bar of justice and tried for offences that nobody knew existed. That is why the learned judges saw fit to require that before a conviction was possible, the order in council concerned must be filed as part of the evidence. I ask the minister to reconsider and repent in reference to this matter.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1977 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
Perhaps I might take a few moments in which to deal with both these proposed amendments. The first is motion No. 7 which would change the meaning of "peace officer". The definition in the bill was put there at the expressed request of a number of provincial attorneys general who wished to restrict the general Criminal Code meaning of "peace officer" which includes deputy sheriffs, justices of the peace and others. Under the Criminal Code as it currently reads, provincial attorneys general have no authority to limit the ability of these people to carry side-arms. I am responding to the expressed request of a number of attorneys general in the amendment I am proposing. After all, they are the chief law enforcement officers in
June 30, 1977

their provinces, and I believe it is incumbent upon this House to take their representations into account. The amendment of the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) would go contrary to the expressed request of the provincial attorneys general.
With regard to motion No. 28, the one which I believe the hon. member regards as being more important, I would say, first of all, that is was moved in committee and debated there and that the hon. member for Calgary North could not carry even his own members on that one. For example, there was disagreement on the part of the distinguished co-chairman of the standing committee on statutory instruments. As hon. members know, all regulations passed by the governor in council stands permanently referred to the committee on statutory instruments for examination. That committee published an excellent report some time ago calling attention to improvements which should be made in the process of delegating legislation, its examination, and so on. Some of those recommendations have been accepted and the government is working on others. However, the responsibility for dealing with this matter lies, surely, with the statutory instruments committee, and our attention should be directed toward improving the processes followed in the examination and supervision of statutory instruments.
I must resist this amendment as a matter of principle. It was on this ground that it was not supported in the committee by the co-chairman of the statutory instruments committee. It would require that every order in council not only be laid before the House-I do not think there would be any great objection to that-but that it should be the subject of an affirmative resolution. I take this to mean that every order in council passed under the Criminal Code would have to be debated in the House. I see an hon. member shaking his head. He had better read the amendment carefully, because that is what it provides. This is a process of supervising regulations which has not even been suggested by the statutory instruments committee, a body which has a very deep and conscientious interest in this matter.

speechtext: May I rise on a question of privilege? 1 know the Minister of Justice has not done this deliberately, but he has misquoted me. I am sorry. 1 was not trying to mislead the House. I meant to say, "under the Criminal Code", and I thought 1 had done so. In drawing up Bill C-51 we were conscious of the criticism which had been raised to the effect that there were too many areas covered by regulation. I believe that any impartial examiner of Bill C-51 would agree with me now that we have markedly reduced the areas of regulation and that the bulk of the regulations to be passed will relate to dealers and manufacturers. As I explained in committee, it is proposed to appoint chief provincial fire-arms officers who
Criminal Code
would become part of a national advisory committee to which would be attached representatives of the dealers and the gun sports. I have undertaken expressly to consult with this committee on the drawing up and making of the regulations. This, in my view, is an effective way of dealing with the matter. It would seem to me that these arrangements, together with the safeguards provided by the normal processes of the statutory instruments committee, are sufficient to meet the hon. member's objections. Provision is made for input into regulationmaking by those interested in gun sports and in the sale of guns, while the work of the statutory instruments committee ensures that the Bill of Rights applies to all these regulations, together with some 18 other considerations which the committee takes into account.
I indicated last week that most of the regulatory power relates to dealers. We have already consulted the Retail Merchants Association, the Transport Association, the Association of Hardware Merchants, and others concerned with those parts of the bill which will be affected by regulation. They have indicated no objection to the provisions of this bill and appear to be satisfied with my undertaking as to the nature of the consultative process to be engaged in. If there is concern about regulatory powers generally, it should be expressed in the debate on the report which the statutory instruments committee published some time ago, and efforts should be made to ensure that the processes followed by that committee are as satisfactory as possible.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1977 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) says he resists these amendments. Well, he resists all amendments or requirements of a nature calculated to restrict the severity of legislation. I do not say this of him personally. It is an attitude he takes in his official capacity. He tells us that the provincial attorneys general have been consulted and have made suggestions. I agree there should be consultation with the attorneys general and that consideration should be given to their points of view. But in some ways they are interested parties, and in the final analysis what has to be taken into account are the views of members of this House. Theoretically, we should be involved. As I recall it, the opening words of the statute are, "Her Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and the House of Commons"-not, "Her Majesty by and with the advice and consent of the attorneys general of the provinces of Canada".
The minister made a very reasonable attempt to rebut the proposition advanced by my eloquent and learned friend from Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams). He said that this is just a little entry that we are making, through the use of orders in council, regulations and delegated authority, to the criminal law. But it is from these little things, Mr. Speaker, that great ones grow. My reading of history tells me that during the First World War an act was brought in known as the Temporary War Income Tax Act. That has grown into one of the greatest monsters with the capacity to eat up so much of the economy of this country. The Temporary War Income Tax Act of 1914

June 30, 1977
Criminal Code
or 1915 has become something which today probably not more than a dozen people in Canada readily understand.
This small beginning, this small entry to the Criminal Code through the use of orders in council and regulations which the Minister of Justice talks about, would, I suggest, if allowed to go unchecked, ten years from now amount to something which, as my hon. friend from Calgary North said, would mean we are legislating by order in council and by delegated authority a large part of our criminal law. As a matter of fact, with the powers the government now has in using governor general's warrants, orders in council, the War Measures Act if necessary, the Anti-Inflation Board, this parliament would not need to meet at all were it not for the fact that the constitution says parliament has to meet. So I am concerned about this trend.
Having said that, 1 suggest to the Minister of Justice that he examine the recent testimony which was given in the last two or three days by Sir Robert Speed, the very learned, eloquent and able member of what 1 might call the establishment of the House of Commons at Westminster, who has had great experience of this whole question of orders in council. The Minister of Justice will be derelict in his duty if he does not read that evidence in the very near future. I see the minister is not listening to me, so I will just continue my remarks and put them on record.
I had the pleasure of meeting Sir Robert Speed some ten years ago when this whole process of statutory instruments was being initiated here. I met him following discussions with the then Prime Minister, the late Mr. Pearson, having had an indication that Mr. Pearson was at least willing to consider some amendments to the statute law of this land to permit the House to take cognizance of the serious problem created by the undue use of orders in council. I was present at two or three meetings of the scrutiny committee in the United Kingdom and observed the very reasonable way in which they dealt with this whole question.
There had developed in the bureaucracy in the United Kingdom an equally reasonable response; in a great many instances all that was necessary was for Sir Robert Speed, who was counsel to the scrutiny committee, to pick up the telephone and to say, "Look, Mr. Parliamentary Secretary, I have just seen a number of orders in council that you are proposing to pass, and I want to point out some mistakes in them." For example, they had an unusual or unexpected impact, or were contrary to natural justice, or they had a retroactive effect, or they were not consistent with the enabling powers in the statute. In 90 per cent of the cases, after reasonable discussion those orders in council were brought into conformity with the enabling statute. When the scrutiny committee of the House of Commons-which is now a joint committee, by the way-was advised of the real facts, an arrangement was made.
I was also very fascinated by what Sir Robert Speed told us just two days ago, namely, that in most instances the right to enact orders in council for subordinate legislative purposes is usually accompanied by the introduction into the bill of the negative or affirmative resolution principle. The Minister of Justice knows that this proposal is contained in the second

report of the statutory instruments committee, and I think it would have a very salutary effect. Indeed, the House is indebted to the hon. member for Calgary North for putting forward this idea at the present time.
Our distinguished visitor from Britain also mentioned that in the majority of cases, I think he said, statutory instruments are subject either to an affirmative or a negative resolution. Consequently, a great deal more care is taken by those who draft orders in council to ensure that they meet the purposes which the act designated for them, that they are consistent with the principles of natural justice, and that they do not give greater authority to the executive and the bureaucrats than they should.
After all, Mr. Speaker, if a bureaucrat who is designated to draft an order in council under a statute is aware that within two or three months the order in council would be subject to very searching scrutiny by men and women of the House of Commons and House of Lords who have been engaged upon the task for some time, he will attempt to see to it that the order in council meets the proper criteria. Because of this, counsel for Mr. Speaker in the United Kingdom told us there are fewer and fewer cases of statutory instruments being made subject to motions to set them aside or change them-what they call in England "prayers".
This is all my hon. friend from Calgary North is asking. Since the government is determined to incorporate into the criminal law the right to change, alter or add criminal law by means of order in council, then for heaven's sake this essential safeguard must be included in the law so that a committee of the House of Commons and the Senate have the right to scrutinize the order in council before it becomes law by way of an affirmative resolution of the House.
There are a number of cases where it would be exceedingly dangerous to change the criminal law before a committee of the House, and then finally parliament itself, had been given the chance to express approval or disapproval. This parliament has never shown itself to be unnecessarily vigilant in this regard, but as a member of parliament and as a member of the bar for many years I would be most unhappy about giving public servants of any government the right to make substantive law or to vary law having to do with criminal proceedings by order in council unless that process were first checked either by committee or by the House.
The minister should take the time to read the evidence which was presented before the Standing Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments last week. He should examine also what Sir Robert Speed said as to the practice, situation and circumstances in England. Surely we would be foolish not to follow the course adopted there, particularly when one considers the number of years this subject has been dealt with in England.

Mr. Speaker, I rise in support of the amendment before us. I have a couple of
June 30, 1977

questions which perhaps could be answered by the mover. The proposed amendment makes a great deal of sense, particularly in terms of using orders in council in the criminal law. One of my reservations is that under the question of declaring a weapon prohibited there may be some emergency if there is a sudden proliferation of that particular weapon in the country. That may be something of an ongoing danger. But that problem can be cured by the passage of the order in council, publication in the Canada Gazette, which would make it law at that point, and then the submission of the order in council to parliament. My only reservation with regard to the proposal of the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) is with respect to an emergency situation. But that is curable under the terms of the wording itself. The principle he and other hon. members have put forward, of not allowing the government to change the law without parliamentary review, is fundamental to the system under which we live. This amendment is so important to that particular system that I can speak on behalf of my entire party by saying that we wholeheartedly support the change proposed by the hon. member for Calgary North.
Operating in a majority position, the government feels it can do anything with regard to the law. The more order in council provisions we put into the law, the less democracy there will be in this country. We represent ordinary people and not people who have access to the law, and we should have the opportunity of reviewing these orders in council and regulations in this place in order to provide a check on that matter.
As I have said, 1 have a minor reservation about the problem of an emergency situation with a dangerous weapon proliferating in the country. But within the reading of motion No. 28, the hon. member for Calgary North has answered that reservation. The order in council could pass and still be placed before this House in order for us to solve the problem and to have the kind of review which is necessary. I am happy to rise in support of this most excellent amendment.

Having listened to the hon. member today, I am thoroughly convinced that I made the right decision. Fortunately, it has never been a case of criminal law. However, there are some areas in this debate upon which I should like to comment. As a backbencher, I am concerned that a senior statesman of this parliament, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), would stand and speak on a matter which has given him a great deal of agony and concern. Above all others, he has become an expert in this field. Hon. members of this House who paid close attention to his remarks were backbenchers. It is unfortunate the minister is so occupied with this bill. He may speak next week after having read Hansard, particularly the comments of the hon. member for Peace River. In any event, it is disturbing that the minister did not
Criminal Code
concentrate on the statements made by the hon. member for Peace River.
There is provision in this bill to determine a class of peace officer or public officer prescribed by the regulations. I am not concerned only with the fact that it is by regulation; I am concerned with one person's, department's or province's interpretation of a public officer as opposed to another. The criteria may not be the same as far as the standard and quality required, the intelligence, balance and reason needed by someone who is given the responsibility of that role. Added to that is the opportunity to carry a sidearm which may not be uniform across this country.
When I was a student working my way through college, 1 had an opportunity to be employed by a detective agency, the name of which I will leave unmentioned. I was given a job at a meat-packing plant in Toronto where there had been a continuing series of thefts. I was provided with a .38 revolver. I never went down to the RCMP; I never filled out any application form, other than the one presented to me by the manager of the detective agency. I was handed a .38 revolver, with ammunition, and I was supposed to use it if the situation arose. Frankly, the situation did arise, but fortunately not on my shift. The purpose of this bill is to tighten up gun control in order to remove those particular loose areas. Two years ago I had the opportunity to urge two of my constituents to lay charges against a big-game hunter or outfitter in northern British Columbia who had harassed them. He had pointed a pistol at them and intimidated them. The minister has made much to do about his concern for gun control. That was two years ago. These two, hard-pressed constituents were flown repeatedly from Castlegar to Fort Nelson to appear in court, denied the opportunity of their own employment, losing money. The charges were read out in court. The man was charged with two things in this instance, possession of an unlicensed pistol in his possession in other than his dwelling place. He pleaded guilty on the first count. On the second count he said, "My hunting territory is my dwelling place."
The judge did not accept that and charged him with being guilty on both counts. That is a pretty fair assumption. He then proceeded to lecture and admonish the person appearing before him, and concluded by dismissing the case. There was not one dime in terms of a fine. If that is the kind of control we are going to have with the implementation of this bill, it is going to fall flat on its can.
I have asked the minister to indicate to this House how many times there have been prosecutions on the basis of charges of carrying unlicensed weapons, revolvers, or what have you, in the commission of a crime. I asked that question months ago. The minister has not yet responded. Provision is there not only in this bill but in previous ones. However, the provisions have not been carried out as the Canadian people, who want a little order and justice in this country, perceive them to be.
Coming to government secrecy and the eloquent arguments of the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams), I am reminded of a statement made yesterday by the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts) and the document that he tabled in the House. All it says is that we are going to have to slacken off a little bit on government secrecy. It indicates that that little bit is damn little.
The minister is concerned about the standing committee on statutory instruments. He feels that the hon. member for Calgary North is going to create some problems. Having listened to the minister, I feel that if we follow the minister's suggestion it will obfuscate that particular committee. The hon. member for Calgary North indicated that while Canadians sleep, this all-powerful government which seeks to be more powerful drafts orders in council that in a majority of cases never appear in the Canada Gazette. For that matter, who reads the Canada Gazette? Once it is there it is supposed to be engraved in stone, and everybody knows about it.
I recall, in a different context, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) talking about trade and international dealings with the United States. He remarked that the United States was like an elephant and that Canada was like a mouse; that we were subject to the rumblings and twitchings of that, I will not say monster, but mighty beast. I would like to put that analogy in a different context. The Canadian people may well be the mighty beast. If we continue down the trail that this government is leading this country, that mighty beast is going to twitch once more. Indeed, it may well roll over and crush this government by regulation. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question also relates to the Solicitor General's role in security matters. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not clear what the hon. member means by his question. A letter was sent to the then Solicitor General, asking questions about the alleged second break-in. All I can say is that parliament passed an act in 1974 which laid down strict regulations and guidelines governing the use in court of electronic listening devices used in criminal matters. It gave the Solicitor General authority to issue warrants authorizing wiretaps in matters involving this country's national security. I remind the hon. member that before 1974 we had no law

June 30, 1977
Oral Questions
forbidding the use of electronic listening devices. This entire matter was constantly brought to the attention of the members of the justice and legal affairs committee.
This whole matter was brought to the attention of the justice and legal affairs committee. The commissioner of the RCMP appeared before that committee on June 12, 1973 and explained the position of the force in detail. He stated that the number of cases of electronic surveillance carried out by the force in the ten years preceding 1973 was something like 1,912. The situation was brought to the attention of the parliamentary committee of the day, which was chaired by Your Honour, and it was studied by that committee; other members of that committee included three former provincial attorneys general who are presently sitting in this House. They were completely informed of the practice of the RCMP in the period of time preceding the very strict regulation of wiretapping activities which was enacted by parliament in 1974.

subsubtopic: SECOND BREAK-IN AT L'AGENCE DE PRESSE LIBRE- GOVERNMENT ACTION

speechtext:
I have just explained the practice of the RCMP which was also the practice followed by other police forces in this country prior to the amendments brought in by parliament in 1974 with a view to exercising stricter control over that kind of activity. I have pointed out to the hon. member that there were 1,912 cases of electronic intrusions by the RCMP in that ten-year period and I do not propose to go through the 1,912 cases to indicate who was and who was not the object of electronic intrusions at that time.
The hon. member will surely understand that it has never been the practice of any previous Solicitor General or Minister of Justice to indicate who was or who was not the object of electronic surveillance in the period prior to 1974. After 1974, parliament enacted certain guidelines and imposed certain obligations under which notification has to be given, and those amendments have led to a vastly improved situation compared with that which existed prior to 1974. 1 believe they have met with the general approval of hon. members.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: SECOND BREAK-IN AT L'AGENCE DE PRESSE LIBRE- GOVERNMENT ACTION

It would appear that the Solicitor General did not understand the question I put to him; it is a simple one and even the hon. gentleman should be able to comprehend it. In view of the fact that he has had adequate notice since last Monday, that the Minister of Justice acknowledged the receipt of a letter by the Solicitor General at the time from the APLQ, I am asking specifically what steps the solicitor general at that time took in connection with that inquiry-the hon.

gentleman need not tell me the object of the surveillance; we can surmise that ourselves. I want to know what was the role of the solicitor general with respect to matters of security which were brought to his attention, what direction he gave to the RCMP. That is a simple question. I do not want any of this statistical stuff. I am just asking what happened in this case.

As to the policy at that time, I would refer him to the proceedings of the House of Commons committee on justice and legal affairs for June 12, 1973. He would see, in reading those proceedings, that the policy of the force was explained in detail. There is even additional information as to how many convictions resulted from those wiretaps.
As to the specific question of the action taken by my predecessor at that time, this matter was brought to his attention and he discussed it to his entire satisfaction with members of the RCMP.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1977 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few comments with respect to motion No. 28 which stands in the name of the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams). I endorse the remarks he made so eloquently before lunch, and also the learned and reasoned argument of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin).
Basically the Criminal Code of Canada provides for law and order in our country and sets the guidelines which affect every man, woman and child. I suggest that the citizens of Canada are entitled to know what the criminal law is, and for that reason the law should be contained within the sections of the Code, or alternatively in regulations that have been approved after debate in this House. I like to think that we live in a democratic country where we have respect for the freedom of the individual and where a person is considered innocent until

proven guilty, and also that there is freedom of information as was discussed this morning by the hon. member for Peace River.
What happens when we begin to be ruled by regulation- regulations which the hon. member for Calgary North said are quite often prepared in the dark of the night without anyone's knowledge? I am not saying that we do not require provisions that enable the Governor in Council to make regulations. Certainly it would be foolish in this day and age to have all the regulations that are promulgated brought before the House for debate. Regulations made under the Criminal Code, however, should by their nature be subject to the scrutiny of parliamentarians.
Having regulations presented in parliament, as is suggested in the motion, would give parliamentarians an opportunity to debate them. When a matter is debated in the House of Commons it becomes the subject of public knowledge through television, radio, and newspaper, and people then have an opportunity to let their members of parliament know their views on the matter. The amendment of the hon. member for Calgary North proposes that within 15 days after regulations have been promulgated they be presented to the House of Commons.
We are not asking for a parliamentary debate on all regulations passed under the various acts, but we are asking that the regulations promulgated under the provisions of the Criminal Code be brought to the House for debate.
I practised law for some 20 years before coming to this House and I know it is very difficult at times to find out exactly what regulations exist. I appreciate that they are printed from time to time in the Canada Gazette, or if they are provincial regulations they are printed in the provincial Gazette, but how many people have the opportunity or the time to read them and find out what regulations have been passed?
Let me give an example of what happened in the province of Saskatchewan with respect to the metric bill. Through the influence of federal civil servants from Ottawa, civil servants of the province of Saskatchewan were able to have promulgated in that province regulations which changed the method of measuring land within the province from acres to hectares. Almost one year after the regulations were passed someone asked a minister of the province and a legislative member a question pertaining to the regulations, and was surprised to discover they did not know those regulations had been passed.
Cabinet ministers are supposed to know what regulations the Governor in Council passes. Presumably they are discussed in cabinet, but in this day and age when we pass so many regulations, ministers understandably have no time to read all of them. Mr. Speaker, it could happen that a regulation is passed without the public's being aware of it until someone is in breach of that regulation, after which it becomes public knowledge.
June 30, 1977

The criminal law of Canada is basic law, and the Code is probably one of the most important statutes in our statute books. If the Governor in Council can pass regulations which amend that law, there is something wrong with our system of government. That is why I urge members of this House to read motion No. 28, for they will see that it asks that all regulations made under the Criminal Code be brought before this House for consideration. In that process parliamentarians could debate them, and members of the public concerned about our criminal law would have the opportunity to make their views known on the acceptability of the regulations.
The hon. member for Calgary North has proposed an excellent amendment. I ask all hon. members who are at all concerned for our democratic way of life to support it.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1977 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, want to speak in support of the amendment. Although not legally trained I can understand how difficult it is to obey a law of which the public is unaware. The previous speaker spoke of orders in council which have the force of law. It is true that cabinet ministers and members of parliament should be aware of changes in the law, yet all too often a minister signs a document placed before him and so gives legal sanction to an order in council without being fully aware of its contents.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) suggested it is not necessary to table orders in council changing the criminal law because the statutory instruments committee scrutinizes all such changes in legislation. He suggested, 1 think, that it is not advantageous to make all such changes public. But the amendment asks more than that. It says that not only should such changes in the law be made public but, since they concern the criminal law, parliament should be given a chance to scrutinize them within 15 days of enactment, or 15 days after a session of parliament begins. This will allow parliament to debate them and either accept them or reject them. 1 suggest the Minister of Justice forgets that many regulations have a greater effect than the original enabling legislation.
That we may wish to outlaw certain guns is not the important point of the amendment. When we debate such questions we are really debating how regulations will be interpreted and enforced. 1 have heard members argue about the length of guns, but that is not a legislative matter. We decide in principle if we are to allow people to possess rapid firing guns, hand guns, or guns easily concealed. In the final analysis, questions as to whether guns of a certain calibre or of a certain type come within the prohibited class are determined through an interpretation of the law. The courts interpret laws, orders in council and other regulations, and acts accordingly. Really, we are enacting a prohibition against handguns, but it has been in effect for some years. We are adding to the prohibited list certain weapons not previously included under the heading of prohibited weapons. We set down the principle and the court interprets the regulations, which stipulate if guns of a certain calibre or certain length are in the prohibited class. My point is this: I may own a B-B gun of a certain calibre and go hunting with it today, but tomorrow, because the regulations are changed without my knowing it, I could be arrested for
Criminal Code
possessing a prohibited weapon. The point is that I would not know the law had changed.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1977 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext: Right on.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1977 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
Surely it is unfair and stupid to amend regulations without letting the public know, and if the Minister of ^Justice cannot see the logic of making such changes in regulations public, his approach to our administration of justice is unrealistic.
In this country it is difficult to enforce justice. The average person thinks the police are picking on him. They pick on him when he drives, when he doesn't wear his seat belt, or when he commits a parking infraction, and the public views none of these infractions as serious. They are offences, true, but they are responsible for much of the public's animosity toward the police. These minor infractions create much friction.
What is the logic of passing regulations of which the public knows nothing? You can drive down the highway tonight, thinking you are within the speed limit, and be arrested because, without your knowing it, the province by secretly passed order in council reduced the speed limit ten miles an hour. Mr. Speaker, this is possible. You will be unhappy because you did not know the law had changed.
How would you feel if, through a sudden change in the regulations, 12-gauge shotguns or No. 5 shells were outlawed? If you are carrying that kind of gun to a duck hunt, you would be very surprised, very hurt, and very arrested just the same.
The Minister of Justice apparently believes in amending the Criminal Code by regulation, and asks us for authority to do so. Apparently he does not want these things made public, and in my view this is disgraceful and out of keeping with the principle of British justice. It may be he can go far in the direction he wishes, but it seems to me he is being unfair to the public, to the traditions of his office, and to the legislation which he wishes the public to support. British justice would call for him to go one step further.
Whenever the Criminal Code is amended by regulation or by order in council or any other of the statutory tools which the government uses, a reference should be made to parliament so that the representatives of the public might have their say. In my opinion the minister would have done the legislation a greater service if he had given an undertaking to proceed along these lines and to have allowed, say, for a day's debate on any changes in the Criminal Code. 1 do not believe he would find this proposition unworkable. It would have the additional advantage of helping to make the public aware of any changes which are being made.
I am always surprised to find that ordinary members of parliament, for whom I have a high regard, lose all sense of balance when they become cabinet ministers-all sense of responsibility to their colleagues and to the nation. The only people to whom they show any responsibility are their departmental officials. This is a great loss, because one would hope

June 30, 1977
Criminal Code
they would continue to exercise normal caution when asked to take measures which the general public will not accept. What seems to happen is that public servants put in place regulations which often take us far away from the legislation which was originally passed by parliament, making it difficult for the public or even for members of parliament to detect any continuity in the changes which take place. Governments would be well advised to make every effort to bring to the attention of the public changes which take place affecting their freedoms and rights. A government which does not make a constant effort to do this is, in my opinion, failing to serve the public well.
Some of us have had an opportunity of looking at the green paper put out by the government with regard to the right of the public to secure certain information. That document can be summed up in a very few words-if it is not likely to offend the civil servants or to cause the government any trouble, there is no great objection to information being published. But if there is any danger to civil servants or to the minister, the documents requested will remain secret. Any changes in the Criminal Code affect you and I from time to time-

speechtext: "You and me".

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1977 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext: Very well, "You and me"-Stanley as well as the rest of us. They are quite likely to affect us as individuals. For this reason there should be as free and as open a flow of information as possible, not only because of the basic principle involved here but because it would help the general public to support the legislation we pass here and which must, of necessity, be changed from time to time. If the Criminal Code is to be amended by regulation, some way should be found to bring these changes to the attention of parliament, and the minister should be the first to accept the kind of amendment put forward by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams).

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1977 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my intervention will be quite brief. I cannot let this opportunity go by without saying how much I support the amendment of the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) which asks that when regulations are made they should be tabled in parliament within 15 days and then debated, especially under the section dealing with gun control.
This morning, when I was speaking, when the minister interjected to say I was in favour of regulation because 1 thought the length of gun barrels should be determined by regulation. If the minister wants to take a close look he will see I am certainly against regulating an important law such as this, though I realize the government likes to do most of its business by order in council and by regulation and incorporates this kind of situation in almost every law it brings forward. Anyway, member opposite are going to vote for this and have it included in the bill even though it is against the wishes of most of the people who are directly affected.
The people this gun law will directly affect are against this kind of thing, but knowing the bill is going to be put through

anyway I want to take this opportunity to say 1 am certainly against regulation by order in council. 1 am against regulations such as those proposed by the minister in connection with laws as important as the Criminal Code. Many of the other members of my party who have had legal training have been able to put this position much more eloquently than I am able to do.
In the over-all, Mr. Speaker, I completely agree that an order in council can change the law within a matter of days, and in such a way that many people are affected. As I have said, it could make criminals out of innocent people. They are the ones who usually get the most harassment. They will not know what is happening to them, but just because they do not know the law does not mean that they do not have to comply with the law. If such regulations were brought back to parliament within 15 days and debated, the people of Canada would have a better opportunity of knowing exactly what is going on. That is the way we should treat the people of this country. In closing, may I say I am strongly in favour of the amendment and I hope my hon. friends opposite will see the logic of it, though I am not too sure they will.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1977 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to add my support for this amendment. The hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) has made a valid point, something worthy of considerable thought when we contemplate our parliamentary procedure. We seem to want to cure problems these days by centralization. Recently a report on broadcasting suggested that broadcasting be brought under one company or operated under one network, which may have a point but nevertheless shows the tendency today toward centralization. More and more we want government to intervene in our lives. We are presently studying a competition bill which, if it is passed, will enable government to intervene further in our private lives and in private business.
This brings me to the point that the bureaucrats, who must of necessity administer legislation, are being given a great deal of power, and I do not think we have properly addressed ourselves to the question of how to curtail some of the excesses which are bound to occur, since these bureaucrats are just as human as we are. Sometimes regulations are made without much thought being given to them; they are made on the spur of the moment, and sometimes the bureaucracy is not even aware of what is happening out in the hinterland. Perhaps they cannot be faulted for that. After all, a minister is probably far too busy to be aware of everything going on in his department, and one cannot expect otherwise. Nevertheless, we should try to do what we can to scrutinize orders in council before they are passed.
I understand that over 3,000 orders in council were passed last year by the federal government, and in addition many were passed in the provincial field. We have recently been discussing metrication, and the MLA's in my own province were unaware that the government of Manitoba had already introduced the metric system in the surveying field. I understand a similar situation exists in Saskatchewan.

June 30, 1977

This amendment provides a means whereby there would be a fairly routine laying on the table of regulations and orders in council in a specified form. I am sure that 99 per cent would go unchallenged, but at least they would be readily available so parliamentarians would observe them. No doubt some members of parliament would find something out of line in an order in council, and although this would not occur very often it would at least eliminate any untoward orders in council. I think this procedure would be a salutary one, those who draft these orders in council, who would have to be more sure of themselves, and in regard to making members of parliament take an interest in orders in council which affect their constituents.
I am not a lawyer, Mr. Speaker, but I understand that it is important that orders in council having to do with the Criminal Code be closely scrutinized. Although this can be said to be the case in all areas of government, it is particularly so in the case of the Criminal Code which needs to be clear and direct. I do not see how the adoption of this amendment would in any way change the Criminal Code as such. In this day and age when we are complaining about secrecy in government, when we are unfamiliar with the vast amounts of orders in council which are passed and with regulations which must necessarily issue from the various departments, this is a welcome departure and may well serve as a model upon which to base further legislative action.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1977 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 intend to enter this debate only briefly to deal with questions which have arisen on the motion of the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams). This amendment merely seeks to provide the vehicle by which parliament has some access to decisions regarding legislation which are taken behind the green, felt covered doors of government orders in council.
The interesting thing is that this debate has not been exclusively confined to lawyers, as is quite often the case when the Criminal Code is discussed. The hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ritchie) who last spoke is a medical doctor. The member who preceded him is a leader in what I guess 1 could call the tender fruit industry of British Columbia. Perhaps this is indicative of the fact that the concern which exists regarding the attitude of government generally respecting orders in council is now spreading beyond the legal profession to members of the Canadian public who have not been burdened with a legal education. I think that is very important.
There is no doubt that one of the things which concerns anyone living in a free society is the tendency today for government not to disclose information, or to be hesitant to do so, particularly government in the Canadian parliamentary system, hampered as we are in terms of information by the doctrine of ministerial responsibility which is only observed when it is convenient to do so. This is buttressed by the document released yesterday by the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts), the green paper on freedom of information, which has been condemned generally as not pointing the way to freedom of information at all, but contains much finer lan-
Criminal Code
guage than heretofore sustaining the rights of government not to disclose.
It becomes extremely important when the statute parliament is dealing with is an amendment to the Criminal Code. It is not an amendment to the Weights and Measures Act nor an amendment to the Small Loans Act. It is an amendment to the Criminal Code, the effect of which can deal with the lives of all subjects in one way or another. Protection has been given to everyone-the blackest and the whitest among us in terms of reputation-by the doctrine that one is presumed innocent until proven otherwise. The same buttress against authority, or the same kind of protection, is intended by the hon. member for Calgary North. He is not saying that governments cannot act by orders in council and that there is not a place for orders in council. There is a place for orders in council in a complex society. We have to change our procedures in terms of the House of Commons, and governments have a great myriad of problems to deal with as well.
The hon. member is saying in his amendment that when there are orders in council passed under this unusual statute, this parliament should be apprised of them; that they should be made known to parliament as the people's representatives; that they should be tabled in the House; and that parliament should have an opportunity to deal with them, just as it would deal with any amendment to the Criminal Code. We are now openly discussing an amendment to the Criminal Code in this House. If there is no reason on the face of orders in council as to why they ought not to be dealt with, then they would not be dealt with and would stand. If there is some reason on the face of orders in council for dealing with them, then they would be dealt with.
The hon. member for Calgary North has not made an unreasonable case. The amendment calls for the order in council to be laid before parliament within 15 days after it is made, and if parliament is not sitting, then 15 days after parliament begins to sit.
The amendment continues as follows:
... every order in council, regulation, or form shall be subject to affirmative resolution of parliament and shall not come into force until published in the Canada Gazette.
That does not say anything, except this: in a subject matter as important as criminal law, the Parliament of Canada ought to have the say and ought to be able to review what bureaucracies have done, even though orders in council can be signed by someone other than a bureaucrat, which is not an unusual or improper suggestion to make to the House. That is the purpose of it, and I hope the government will support it. If it does not support it, I have to ask myself why not?
Perhaps there are a number of members of this House who disagree with this, including members of my party; but I cannot understand why the very important procedure of an affirmative resolution is alien to the thinking of some members. I hope hon. members on the other side will not vote against the amendment because it happens to be an opposition

amendment. Whether we support a government or whether we are members of an opposition, members ought to look at the rights of each of us as representatives of the people.
I am aware of the doctrine that everyone is deemed to know the law. That is great for lawyers, that is great if you happen to know the law, and it is necessary for the proper administration of justice. But it is a devil of a thing for the fellow who is innocently caught in a situation, which can happen quite often.
I shall conclude my remarks because I do not believe there is another speaker from this side of the House and I do not want to hold up consideration of this amendment. I hope hon. members on the other side of the House will consider the propriety of the amendment and the spirit in which it is moved. Even though there may be members on either side of the Chair who disagree with the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Calgary North, I hope they reconsider their opposition to this important amendment.
